papers.abstract: Controlling generative models without access to paired or disentangled data remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in domains where attributes such as style are inherently entangled with content. We introduce latent trace guidance, a general framework for controllable generation that operates by aligning a model’s internal representations with an external guidance signal expressed in a compatible latent space. Unlike conventional conditioning or activation steering, the proposed approach does not require explicit supervision or attribute labels, and allows guidance signals to originate from arbitrary sources, provided they can be mapped into the model’s representation space via an adapter. To isolate the core mechanism, we study a pure-form instantiation in the context of symbolic melodic harmonization, where guidance is derived directly from the model’s own latent representations and re-applied during generation. This setting enables a controlled comparison with activation steering across architectures and cross-style scenarios. Experimental results show that latent trace guidance consistently improves alignment with target stylistic characteristics and, in several cases, outperforms activation steering, particularly when counteracting strong model biases. These findings highlight latent-space alignment as a promising direction for controllable generation beyond explicitly supervised settings.

papers.title: LiveBand: Live Accompaniment Generation in the Audio Domain
papers.authors: Marco Pasini; Javier Nistal; Mathias R. Bjare; Stefan Lattner; György Fazekas
papers.abstract: We present LiveBand, a real-time system that generates high-fidelity music accompaniments to live audio input, respecting strict causal constraints. Our method trains a causal transformer generator in the continuous latent space of a pre-trained causal audio autoencoder, using adversarial sequence-level supervision from a discriminator. At each timestep, the generator receives only the causally available mix context and Gaussian noise, and predicts accompaniment latents without access to future mix frames or ground-truth target latents. Training is performed in a single parallel forward pass under causal masking, while streaming inference proceeds autoregressively with a rolling attention state. The model’s training and inference computations are matched by design, eliminating teacher forcing and the associated exposure bias. On a multi-instrument music accompaniment benchmark, LiveBand improves over prior work on objective measures of audio quality, beat alignment, and mix adherence, while enabling real-time streaming generation without lookahead into the future on consumer hardware.

papers.title: Soft Late-Fusion Alignment and Pattern-Based Performance Analysis of Early 20th-Century Solo Flute Music
papers.authors: Patrice Thibaud; Louis Bigo; Mathieu Giraud; Yann Teytaut
papers.abstract: This paper investigates expressive timing in solo flute performances of early 20th-century repertoire through curated data, audio-to-audio alignment, and pattern-level analysis. We introduce a corpus of 23 performances each of Debussy’s Syrinx and Varèse’s Density 21.5, enabling the study of timing in flexible metronomic contexts. A subset of recordings is manually annotated at the onset level and used as a reference to propagate annotations to the remaining performances via a multi-reference audio-to-audio alignment framework. We extend existing late-fusion strategies to onset-level transfer and introduce a soft weighting scheme based on triple-alignment consistency, replacing hard reference selection with a continuous reliability measure. This improves the stability of onset estimates across heterogeneous interpretations. We further propose a pattern-level framework for expressive timing that extends beyond beat-based representations, enabling systematic comparison of duration and timing fluctuations in both cell- and phrase-level patterns. This allows us to investigate whether performers realise these patterns consistently or variably across different levels of musical organisation. Overall, the proposed pipeline supports the alignment, propagation, and analysis of expressive timing in repertoires with flexible metronomic structure.

papers.authors: Riccardo Simionato; Louis Bigo
papers.abstract: Guitar tablature transcription requires not only accurate pitch detection but also assigning each note to a specific string-fret position, as the same pitch can be played at multiple fretboard positions. Existing approaches treat this as a standard classification problem, ignoring the musical and physical constraints that govern playable fingering sequences. We propose Noise2Fret, a diffusion model for audio-to-tablature transcription that generates tablature through a continuous latent representation of discrete fret and string targets, conditioned on spectral and audio features. To bridge the gap between pitch accuracy and physical playability, we introduce five auxiliary losses encoding Pitch-Class Distance, Positional Distance, Circle-of-Fifths Distance, String Similarity, and Hand-Span Feasibility directly into the training objective. Experiments on GuitarSet and GOAT datasets demonstrate that the model outperforms baselines while remaining computationally more efficient, and that the auxiliary losses yield consistent gains over the standard training objective.

papers.authors: Anıl Tuncel
papers.abstract: This paper presents OudTabs, a microtonal oud tablature representation, a cross-tradition symbolic corpus, and an interactive software platform for makam-family and related modal repertoires. Its underlying representation aims to diversify music research beyond Western staff notation by grounding itself in the oud’s fingerboard, preserving each tradition’s native pitch system, modal vocabulary, and rhythmic categories. Every note is encoded as string, position, and duration on the instrument, with pitch expressed as exact frequency-derived fractional positions in cents. The same cent-level values drive both the visual display and the audio, so learners and researchers hear each microtone at its target pitch while simultaneously seeing it as a concrete location on the oud. This cent-level resolution lets the OudTabs representation capture microtonal intonation more finely than the notations commonly used in oud teaching. Built on this foundation, we release the OudTabs Corpus, a cross-tradition tablature corpus of 3,672 pieces and 1,957,167 note events unified from heterogeneous public symbolic corpora, made playable, searchable, and audible through an interactive playback and browsing system. Together, these contributions provide new infrastructure for pedagogy, computational musicology, and future MIR research on microtonal oud music.

papers.abstract: Recognized as the first East Asian system to jointly encode pitch and rhythm, Jeongganbo notation represents a landmark in musicology and has been used in the Korean musical tradition since the 15th century. As a result, a vast amount of music content exists only in physical sheet form and is currently threatened by deterioration. Digitisation efforts have successfully archived these scores as digital images, but the lack of machine-readable transcriptions restricts their use by computational tools. Although Optical Music Recognition (OMR) offers a solution to automate this transcription, existing research on Jeongganbo has relied exclusively on software-rendered scores, which fail to capture the complexities of real documents. To address this limitation, this work presents two main contributions: (i) a new dataset comprising five handwritten Jeongganbo score books and 403 pages, along with their corresponding annotations for OMR tasks; and (ii) a two-step Deep Learning pipeline for full-page recognition of these scores. The results of a rigorous cross-domain evaluation of the methodology studied show competitive performance, while also providing useful insights into the design choices of Jeongganbo OMR systems. papers.title: On the use of Pre-trained Audio Encoders for Audio-to-Score Music Transcription
papers.authors: Antonio Hidalgo-Centeno; Carlos Penarrubia; Jose J. Valero-Mas
papers.abstract: Audio-to-Score (A2S) transcription, a recent paradigm within Automatic Music Transcription (AMT), converts acoustic music recordings into score-level representations in a single step. These approaches primarily rely on end-to-end deep neural architectures, which avoid error propagation in multi-stage score-oriented AMT systems. However, they require large collections of music recordings paired with annotated scores, which are severely limited due to the substantial manual effort and expert knowledge required for their creation. Drawing inspiration from related domains, this work investigates the use of pre-trained audio encoders to mitigate this limitation and improve transcription accuracy. Specifically, we evaluate six encoders from different domains—including music, speech, and general audio processing—and assess their capabilities for music transcription. These findings suggest that pre-trained audio models are a promising direction for advancing A2S transcription and reducing dependence on large annotated datasets.

papers.title: Integrating Contextual Embeddings into Evaluation of Expressive MIDI Piano Performances
papers.authors: Dmitrii Gavrilev; Ilya Borovik; Vladimir Viro
papers.abstract: Objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances typically relies on attribute statistics such as timing, velocity, and duration of individual notes. However, these methods often disregard dependencies between notes, which poses a potential limitation in assessing the similarity between two sets of performances. In generative applications, the wide variety of expressive attributes makes it difficult to aggregate them into a single scalar metric for model selection. In this work, we reexamine attribute-scoped metrics and explore the perceptual properties of contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models, Aria and CLaMP3. Results from our listening study indicate that these models can be used as perceptual proxies, showing agreement with per-sample human ratings on par with traditional metrics. Unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error, kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations. papers.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
papers.authors: Bánk Juhász; Gerhard Widmer; Jan Schlüter
papers.abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. papers.title: Latent Trace Guidance for Generative Control Without Disentangled Data in Symbolic Melodic Harmonization
papers.authors: Maximos Kaliakatsos-Papakostas; Dimos Makris; Konstantinos-Theodoros Tsamis; Konstantinos Soiledis; Vassilis Katsouros
papers.abstract: Controlling generative models without access to paired or disentangled data remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in domains where attributes such as style are inherently entangled with content. Unlike conventional conditioning or activation steering, the proposed approach does not require explicit supervision or attribute labels, and allows guidance signals to originate from arbitrary sources, provided they can be mapped into the model’s representation space via an adapter. This setting enables a controlled comparison with activation steering across architectures and cross-style scenarios. papers.authors: Marco Pasini; Javier Nistal; Mathias R. Bjare; Stefan Lattner; György Fazekas
papers.abstract: We present LiveBand, a real-time system that generates high-fidelity music accompaniments to live audio input, respecting strict causal constraints. papers.title: Soft Late-Fusion Alignment and Pattern-Based Performance Analysis of Early 20th-Century Solo Flute Music
papers.authors: Patrice Thibaud; Louis Bigo; Mathieu Giraud; Yann Teytaut
papers.abstract: This paper investigates expressive timing in solo flute performances of early 20th-century repertoire through curated data, audio-to-audio alignment, and pattern-level analysis. To bridge the gap between pitch accuracy and physical playability, we introduce five auxiliary losses encoding Pitch-Class Distance, Positional Distance, Circle-of-Fifths Distance, String Similarity, and Hand-Span Feasibility directly into the training objective. Experiments on GuitarSet and GOAT datasets demonstrate that the model outperforms baselines while remaining computationally more efficient, and that the auxiliary losses yield consistent gains over the standard training objective.

papers.authors: Anıl Tuncel
papers.abstract: This paper presents OudTabs, a microtonal oud tablature representation, a cross-tradition symbolic corpus, and an interactive software platform for makam-family and related modal repertoires. Every note is encoded as string, position, and duration on the instrument, with pitch expressed as exact frequency-derived fractional positions in cents. The same cent-level values drive both the visual display and the audio, so learners and researchers hear each microtone at its target pitch while simultaneously seeing it as a concrete location on the oud. This cent-level resolution lets the OudTabs representation capture microtonal intonation more finely than the notations commonly used in oud teaching. Built on this foundation, we release the OudTabs Corpus, a cross-tradition tablature corpus of 3,672 pieces and 1,957,167 note events unified from heterogeneous public symbolic corpora, made playable, searchable, and audible through an interactive playback and browsing system. Together, these contributions provide new infrastructure for pedagogy, computational musicology, and future MIR research on microtonal oud music.

papers.authors: Zixun Guo; Simon Dixon

papers.authors: George Sioros

A few cycles require different but closely related configurations for comparable residual errors. papers.title: Unified Music Identification for Tracks and Versions
papers.authors: R. Oguz Araz; Joan Serrà; Yuki Mitsufuji; Xavier Serra; Dmitry Bogdanov
papers.abstract: Given a music database, track identification (TI) retrieves the exact track matching an audio excerpt, whereas version identification (VI) retrieves its musical versions. Traditionally, the two tasks have been addressed separately. However, as every track is its own closest version, we investigate whether VI can subsume TI. This requires VI systems to be robust to both signal manipulation and audio degradation. We therefore propose a unified benchmark that evaluates accuracy and robustness on each task. Comparing seven existing models on this benchmark, we show that none of them are both accurate and robust on both tasks. We then train a baseline model targeting both tasks and show that a unified system is possible with 10 s TI queries. Lastly, we characterize the two retrieval constraints that limit our model’s TI performance. We envision extending this unification to other music identification tasks.

papers.authors: Alejandro Galan-Cuenca; Juan P. Martinez-Esteso; Carlos Pérez-Sancho; Francisco J. Castellanos; Antonio Javier Gallego
papers.abstract: Pixel-level annotation of music score images is essential for training reliable Optical Music Recognition and document analysis systems, but it remains a time-consuming task that requires expert intervention. This paper presents PixelSmart, an open-source AI-assisted annotation tool for music score layout analysis. Instead of annotating from scratch, users start from model-generated proposals and focus on correcting and validating them. We evaluate the proposed workflow with five annotators on three music score datasets, comparing it against a general-purpose editor and a specialized manual annotation tool. papers.authors: Yiwei Ding; Yannik Venohr; Sebastian Strahl; Meinard Müller; Christof Weiß
papers.abstract: In the deep-learning era, automatic chord recognition (ACR) from audio predominantly relies on end-to-end strategies. We leverage existing large-scale transcription datasets to pretrain the MPE module and chord-annotated symbolic music datasets to pretrain the chord recognition module, thereby addressing the scarcity of annotated audio data. This allows the MPE module to handle diverse instrumentation and acoustic conditions, and the chord recognition module to capture harmonic diversity. Experiments show that two-stage models consistently outperform end-to-end baselines on Western classical music and that fine-tuning on popular music outperforms end-to-end models trained directly on pop music, demonstrating cross-genre transferability. Our work establishes the two-stage approach as a robust and effective framework for deep-learning-based audio ACR.

papers.title: The Internet Archive Music Dataset
papers.authors: Paraskevas Stamatiadis; Bernardo V. Miranda; Clémentine Berger; Gaël Richard; Mathieu Fontaine; Slim Essid
papers.abstract: We introduce the Internet Archive Music Dataset (IAMD), a large-scale collection of captioned music segments derived from the Internet Archive. To the best of our knowledge, IAMD constitutes the largest publicly available music–caption dataset to date with over 34,000 hours of audio, providing a valuable benchmark for training and evaluating music understanding and generative models. The dataset is built from content declared to be distributed under Creative Commons licenses, and cross-referencing with MusicBrainz is done to improve license information reliability. papers.title: Robust Instrument-Agnostic Music Transcription for Western Classical Music
papers.authors: Yannik Venohr; Christof Weiß
papers.abstract: Musicological corpus analysis from audio, among other scenarios, requires Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) methods that generalize across instrumentations and acoustic conditions. While AMT has advanced substantially, existing methods lack robustness: a model may transcribe high-quality recordings well but fail on noisy historical ones, or have problems with challenging instrumentations such as choir. To study such behavior, we focus on Western classical music as an application domain and compile a large, heterogeneous data scenario from existing datasets. As our main contribution, we introduce ClassicPitch (CP), a CNN model for instrument-agnostic music transcription on the frame and note levels. Rather than introducing a single novel component, CP combines and modernizes established techniques into a coherent and scalable framework: a convolutional frame-level backbone with efficient ConvNeXt blocks, and onsets derived from a shared frame representation. In a variant with under 50K parameters, our model is already superior to substantially larger models on various datasets and evaluation metrics, demonstrating that competitive and robust instrument-agnostic AMT is achievable with a lightweight fully convolutional model. More importantly, CP remains stable on noisy real-world recordings. We publish CP as an open-source, open-weight tool for musical corpus analysis and beyond.

papers.title: "I Just Kept Clicking Until It Hit": Exploring Virtual Instrument Search behavior and Challenges Across User Groups
papers.authors: Subeen Kim; Eunsik Shin; Woojae Cho; Kyogu Lee
papers.abstract: Virtual instrument search is a common yet relatively underexplored bottleneck in music production. Although users often have a clear idea of the sound they want, they differ substantially in how they describe target sounds, navigate preset libraries, and evaluate search results. To better understand these differences, we conducted a mixed-methods study with 33 participants who completed preset-retrieval tasks in Logic Pro's Alchemy followed by semi-structured interviews. Our analysis shows that users can be meaningfully characterized along two dimensions—music domain knowledge and search experience—and that they form four distinct groups for understanding instrument-search users. Across groups, we observed systematic differences in verbal expression, search behavior, perceived system limitations, and desired technical, functional, and interface support. Furthermore, we explored the potential of utilizing free-form text inputs to capture how users' personalized backgrounds uniquely shape their descriptions of virtual instruments. These results suggest that instrument-retrieval systems should support diverse forms of expression and search pathways.

papers.authors: Mathias Rose Bjare; Augustin Bouquillard; Giorgia Cantisani; Seung-Goo Kim; Stefan Lattner, Paris); Gerhard Widmer
papers.abstract: We propose the Musical Expectation (MEX) benchmark suite for perceptually validating computational models of musical expectation, i.e., models that estimate music information dynamics (MID) measures of perceived musical expectations, such as surprisal or uncertainty from symbolic music or musical audio. MEX collects and extends tasks for evaluating such models previously proposed in music information retrieval and cognitive sciences using standard datasets, and evaluates whether: (1) proposed MID measures decrease with repetition due to in-context learning of the computational model, (2) peaks in such measures align with boundaries of music segments, (3) pitch surprisal and uncertainty estimated from audio are consistent with those modeled in event-based symbolic music, (4) proposed MID measures can predict electrophysiological responses to music. We stress that this benchmark suite does not provide an exhaustive computational characterization of music expectation. Rather, we envision this as an active, interdisciplinary initiative, with benchmarks evolving as our understanding of the underlying perceptual processes deepens. We provide open-access code to estimate surprisal and uncertainty from audio using baseline models, run the tasks on standard datasets, and include utilities for running the tasks with users' own data.

papers.title: Understanding Automatic Mixing: A Subtask-Oriented Analysis of Two-Stage Mixing System
papers.authors: Jinjie Shi; Wei Hua; Kunzhu Xie; Make Li; Yuchen Liu; Joshua Reiss
papers.abstract: Automatic mixing transforms multitrack recordings into perceptually coherent, balanced, and aesthetically consistent mixes. Both two-stage variants significantly outperform their corresponding single-stage baselines. These findings support explicit separation of local balance and global mix coordination as a useful design principle for automatic mixing. Code and audio examples are available online.

papers.title: The Internet Archive Music Dataset
papers.authors: Paraskevas Stamatiadis; Bernardo V. Miranda; Clémentine Berger; Gaël Richard; Mathieu Fontaine; Slim Essid
papers.abstract: We introduce the Internet Archive Music Dataset (IAMD), a large-scale collection of captioned music segments derived from the Internet Archive. To the best of our knowledge, IAMD constitutes the largest publicly available music–caption dataset to date with over 34,000 hours of audio, providing a valuable benchmark for training and evaluating music understanding and generative models. The dataset is built from content declared to be distributed under Creative Commons licenses, and cross-referencing with MusicBrainz is done to improve license information reliability. To annotate IAMD, we present an automatic captioning pipeline that augments base captions produced by an audio-language model (ALM) with textual metadata sourced from the Internet Archive and imputed metadata obtained using audio classification models. Caption quality is assessed objectively and subjectively, and results indicate that the annotation pipeline is reliable and does not degrade caption quality with scaling.

papers.title: Robust Instrument-Agnostic Music Transcription for Western Classical Music
papers.authors: Yannik Venohr; Christof Weiß
papers.abstract: Musicological corpus analysis from audio, among other scenarios, requires Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) methods that generalize across instrumentations and acoustic conditions. While AMT has advanced substantially, existing methods lack robustness: a model may transcribe high-quality recordings well but fail on noisy historical ones, or have problems with challenging instrumentations such as choir. To study such behavior, we focus on Western classical music as an application domain and compile a large, heterogeneous data scenario from existing datasets. We perform cross-dataset evaluation on seven held-out test sets, including a recently introduced robustness benchmark. As our main contribution, we introduce ClassicPitch (CP), a CNN model for instrument-agnostic music transcription on the frame and note levels. Rather than introducing a single novel component, CP combines and modernizes established techniques into a coherent and scalable framework: a convolutional frame-level backbone with efficient ConvNeXt blocks, and onsets derived from a shared frame representation. In a variant with under 50K parameters, our model is already superior to substantially larger models on various datasets and evaluation metrics, demonstrating that competitive and robust instrument-agnostic AMT is achievable with a lightweight fully convolutional model. More importantly, CP remains stable on noisy real-world recordings. We publish CP as an open-source, open-weight tool for musical corpus analysis and beyond.

papers.title: "I Just Kept Clicking Until It Hit": Exploring Virtual Instrument Search behavior and Challenges Across User Groups
papers.authors: Subeen Kim; Eunsik Shin; Woojae Cho; Kyogu Lee
papers.abstract: Virtual instrument search is a common yet relatively underexplored bottleneck in music production. Although users often have a clear idea of the sound they want, they differ substantially in how they describe target sounds, navigate preset libraries, and evaluate search results. To better understand these differences, we conducted a mixed-methods study with 33 participants who completed preset-retrieval tasks in Logic Pro's Alchemy followed by semi-structured interviews. Our analysis shows that users can be meaningfully characterized along two dimensions—music domain knowledge and search experience—and that they form four distinct groups for understanding instrument-search users. Across groups, we observed systematic differences in verbal expression, search behavior, perceived system limitations, and desired technical, functional, and interface support. Furthermore, we explored the potential of utilizing free-form text inputs to capture how users' personalized backgrounds uniquely shape their descriptions of virtual instruments. These results suggest that instrument-retrieval systems should support diverse forms of expression and search pathways.

papers.title: MEX: The Musical Expectation Benchmark Suite
papers.authors: Mathias Rose Bjare; Augustin Bouquillard; Giorgia Cantisani; Seung-Goo Kim; Stefan Lattner, Paris); Gerhard Widmer
papers.abstract: We propose the Musical Expectation (MEX) benchmark suite for perceptually validating computational models of musical expectation, i.e., models that estimate music information dynamics (MID) measures of perceived musical expectations, such as surprisal or uncertainty from symbolic music or musical audio. MEX collects and extends tasks for evaluating such models previously proposed in music information retrieval and cognitive sciences using standard datasets, and evaluates whether: (1) proposed MID measures decrease with repetition due to in-context learning of the computational model, (2) peaks in such measures align with boundaries of music segments, (3) pitch surprisal and uncertainty estimated from audio are consistent with those modeled in event-based symbolic music, (4) proposed MID measures can predict electrophysiological responses to music. We stress that this benchmark suite does not provide an exhaustive computational characterization of music expectation. Rather, we envision this as an active, interdisciplinary initiative, with benchmarks evolving as our understanding of the underlying perceptual processes deepens. We provide open-access code to estimate surprisal and uncertainty from audio using baseline models, run the tasks on standard datasets, and include utilities for running the tasks with users' own data.

papers.title: Understanding Automatic Mixing: A Subtask-Oriented Analysis of Two-Stage Mixing System
papers.authors: Jinjie Shi; Wei Hua; Kunzhu Xie; Make Li; Yuchen Liu; Joshua Reiss
papers.abstract: Automatic mixing transforms multitrack recordings into perceptually coherent, balanced, and aesthetically consistent mixes. However, in real-world production, this task is challenging due to large track counts, diverse instrumentation, and strong inter-track dependencies. Two-stage systems address this complexity by separating intra-group processing from inter-group mixing, yet it remains unclear whether their gains arise from stronger component models or from explicit task decomposition. We present a subtask-oriented analysis of automatic mixing through three controlled listening experiments. We investigate whether full-mix models transfer to intra-group mixing, whether downstream models compensate for grouping and loudness errors, and whether two-stage decomposition improves full-mix quality. Across three dense pop and rock excerpts, transfer differs between the evaluated models; inappropriate grouping causes clear downstream degradation, while altered loudness relationships have weaker and model-dependent effects. Both two-stage variants significantly outperform their corresponding single-stage baselines. These findings support explicit separation of local balance and global mix coordination as a useful design principle for automatic mixing. Code and audio examples are available online.

papers.title: Adapting Music Foundation Models to Iranian Classical Music
papers.authors: Pouya Mohseni; Bagher BabaAli; Ichiro Fujinaga
papers.abstract: This work evaluates whether Western-trained music foundation models transfer effectively to the specialized domain of Iranian Classical Music, and compares four adaptation regimes: probing, full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient transfer learning, and continued pre-training. Using a 620-hour corpus of domain-specific audio, we systematically study how much adaptation is required for transfer and when domain-specific pre-training yields meaningful gains. These approaches are benchmarked across five downstream tasks. Our results show that while parameter- and data-efficient methods achieve strong performance on supervised tasks, they exhibit reduced transferability to unseen tasks within the same domain compared to more computationally intensive strategies. Furthermore, we find that continued pre-training is not strictly necessary for competitive downstream performance, although it can improve cross-task transferability without introducing additional inference overhead.

papers.title: SmartLooper: a Framework for Personalized Human-AI Musical Improvisation
papers.authors: Finlay Miller; Sageev Oore; Chandramouli Sastry; Marvin da Silva; Sri Harsha Dumpala; Dani Oore; Scott Lowe
papers.abstract: Real-time human--AI musical collaboration presents a persistent design challenge: AI contributions tend to be either too conservative to be interesting or too unpredictable to play along with. We posit that looping (along with related practices of vamping and grooving) offers a framework that sidesteps this trade-off. These recurring structures bound variation within forms the musician already understands, and let development accrue over musical rather than sample-level timescales---a balance upon which improvisers have long relied when playing with each other. We present SmartLooper, a system for real-time human–AI piano improvisation built on this premise. The performer first assembles a personal corpus of their own loop-based recordings, giving them complete control over the stylistic space the system inhabits. SmartLooper segments this corpus into short loops and embeds them using pretrained MIDI models. In performance, the system improvises by retrieving loops from the corpus via a stochastic walk in embedding space: successive loops are chosen for proximity so that transitions feel continuous. To broaden the corpus without diluting its character, we augment the data with synthetic loops in the style of the corpus generated using MIDI-GPT. These are filtered down to only high-quality samples using a discriminator trained to distinguish degraded MIDI from samples in the personal corpus. The resulting dataset extension provides broader support for fluid transitions while preserving the performer's voice. SmartLooper has been used by professional musicians in over ten hours of live performance for audiences totalling roughly a thousand listeners so far; we provide example recordings.

papers.title: D-Composer: Language Modeling for Simultaneous Drum Transcription and Sound Event Decomposition
papers.authors: Patrick O'Reilly; Saumya Pailwan; Annie Chu; Jason Smith; Bryan Pardo
papers.abstract: Drum beats are often conceptualized and produced as arrangements of repeated single-drum sound events or one-shots. Drum Analysis-by-Synthesis (AbS) models combine this structural assumption with reconstruction-based training to perform MIR tasks such as drum transcription, drum source separation, and one-shot extraction, offering a flexible alternative to more traditional task-specific supervision. However, leading AbS approaches struggle to generalize to a broad range of drum timbres (e.g., electronic drum kits), rely on high-quality paired audio-transcription training data, and do not model intra-class timbral variation within a single arrangement (e.g., multiple kick sounds). To overcome these limitations, we propose D-Composer, an autoregressive language modeling framework that decomposes drum recordings into labeled sound events and their onset times. In drum transcription and one-shot extraction tasks, D-Composer performs comparably to or better than a state-of-the-art AbS system and task-specific baselines while generalizing to a broader range of drum timbres. Our results demonstrate that when equipped with abundant synthetic data and compact acoustic token representations, language modeling provides a simple recipe for unifying transcription and sound event decomposition.

papers.title: CoALa: A Plugin Model for Controlling Audio Latents
papers.authors: Sarah Nabi; Nabarun Goswami; Philippe Esling; Geoffroy Peeters; Frédéric Bevilacqua; Tatsuya Harada
papers.abstract: In recent years, neural audio synthesis has advanced significantly, enabling high-quality real-time waveform generation on standard CPUs. However, defining personalized controls for live musical performance remains challenging, as existing methods typically require large labeled datasets and rely on heavy architectures that are generally impractical for real-time use. In this paper, we propose CoALa, a lightweight plugin model for Controlling Audio Latents in real-time, which enables users to add time-varying musical controls on pretrained neural audio synthesis models using only a limited set of labeled examples. Our method leverages a variational autoencoder with a contrastive learning regularization to disentangle control-relevant features from the pretrained latent space in designated dimensions. We rely on labeled frames as an augmentation strategy to generate multiple views of similar control variations for each unlabeled latent sequence, and apply the contrastive objective on these variation embeddings. By augmenting the pretrained latent space with temporal latent tokens, our method supports an arbitrary number of control variables, generalizes to highly compact latent representations, and can simultaneously disentangle multiple time-varying controls evolving at different temporal scales. Our model defines a bidirectional mapping between latent and control trajectories and achieves high control accuracy while preserving synthesis quality for feature extraction, editing, and conditional synthesis tasks, using as little as 10% labeled data. Its lightweight streamable architecture further enables fast CPU inference, making it well suited for real-time applications in Max/MSP environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/nabsara/coala.

papers.title: MAJEPPA: Morphing and Assessing in a Unified Piano Performance Space
papers.authors: Jinwen Zhou; Huan Zhang; Weixi Zhai; Jinhua Liang; Aidan O. T. Hogg; Simon Dixon
papers.abstract: We present MAJEPPA, a self-supervised framework to learn piano performance representations that span the full skill spectrum, from beginner practice sessions to virtuoso concert recordings. We curate the MAJEPPA dataset, comprising ~4,000 annotated recordings across six expertise levels and six recording contexts. We adapt a single pre-trained MIDI autoregressive model with a joint objective: next-token prediction learns score-conditioned performance generation at various skill levels, while InfoNCE and supervised contrastive losses align abstract score and performance representations in a joint embedding space. The proposed model both generates and understands performances in a unified framework. By introducing the EVPMR benchmark, a suite of downstream tasks spanning quality assessment, competition ranking, mistake and technique classification, we evaluate the learnt representations, demonstrating progress towards a real-world model for the piano performance space.

papers.title: Harmonic Representations in Symbolic Music Transformers are Localized and Controllable
papers.authors: Adi Silberschein; Megan Wei; Tamar Rott Shaham
papers.abstract: Transformer models trained on symbolic music have become remarkably capable. However, it is yet unclear how they represent music structure, and whether understanding their internal representations can be used to unlock methods from model control. We examine this through a case study of harmonic analysis: when a music transformer navigates a cadence, what does it internally ``know'' about its harmonic context, and can that knowledge be used to affect the generation? Using Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer evaluated on Bach chorales, we find that harmonic decisions are causally localized progressively from middle layers onward. Linear probes show that mode becomes decodable in the same layer range where patching identifies growing causal effect, while key identity emerges later. We then confirm these representations are actionable for music generation control: steering via latent directions corresponding to harmonic changes reliably produces a deceptive resolution, while preserving structural coherence and generation quality. This demonstrates that, at inference time, the model's internal harmonic knowledge can be directly manipulated to control the harmonic output.

papers.title: From Prediction to Collaboration: Interactive Symbolic Music Analysis
papers.authors: Emmanouil Karystinaios; Johannes Hentschel; Markus Neuwirth; Gerhard Widmer
papers.abstract: Automatic symbolic music analysis has made substantial progress, yet existing systems are typically designed for a single mode of use, such as full-score prediction, and therefore do not match the broader range of operations that arise in analysis workflows, including partial completion, local correction, and iterative refinement. As a result, there remains a gap between strong benchmark models and systems that can support interactive analytical use. We present a unified framework for symbolic Roman-numeral (RN) analysis that narrows this gap by combining strong predictive performance with direct support for constrained completion and revision. The method is designed to provide a practical trade-off between accuracy and interactive responsiveness by computing expensive pretrained representations once and reusing them during iterative refinement, making powerful pretrained models more amenable to interactive settings. It supports complete score analysis, targeted revision of existing labels, and inference of missing annotations from partial context through a shared modeling framework. Experiments on Dilemmadata, the largest and most heterogeneous benchmark of its kind, show that the proposed approach is a strong RN-analysis baseline while also supporting masked completion from partial labels. Together with a prototype interface for multi-level candidate inspection and editing, these results position automatic RN analysis not only as a prediction problem, but also as a foundation for future interactive tools for music analysis.

papers.title: A First Benchmark and Metric for Evaluating Polyphony in Symbolic Music using Voice Independence
papers.authors: Eleanor Row; György Fazekas
papers.abstract: Polyphony in symbolic music is often measured by vertical note density or other basic objective metrics. Such metrics, however, fail to account for voice independence and counterpoint textures that are central to musicology. We introduce a compact, musically informed benchmark dataset for evaluating multi-part polyphony: Polyphony-Ranked Excerpt Dataset (PolyRED), alongside a proposed metric: the Polyphonic Voice Independence Index (PVII). PolyRED comprises rankings of 15 four-part excerpts from three domains: Bach chorales, classical and modern string quartets, annotated by 25 score-literate musicians. Agreement was moderate across the evaluation trials (mean Kendall’s W=0.58, rising to 0.64 in sensitivity analysis). These rankings were then used to derive pairwise win-rate reference scores, serving as human-derived benchmark targets for evaluating new metrics. PVII quantifies independence through similarity between melodic, rhythmic, and onset-based part representations. On this compact benchmark, PVII produced rankings that were more closely aligned with aggregated score-literate participant rankings than density- and overlap-based baselines. These results provide initial evidence that voice-independence features capture aspects of perceived polyphony in short, four-part, predominantly monophonic symbolic textures.

papers.title: CapCyCin: Improving Music Captioning through Cycle-Consistent Music–Text Alignment
papers.authors: Saeyeon Hwang; Kyungsu Kim; Kyogu Lee
papers.abstract: Music captioning is inherently ambiguous as there is no single correct description for a given music. This makes it difficult to define and evaluate what should be considered a good caption. Existing audio captioning metrics often fail to capture semantic equivalence across diverse captions and may not always provide accurate scores for semantically inconsistent descriptions. In addition, human evaluation is costly and subjective. To address these limitations, we propose CapCyCin, a Cycle-Consistency-based framework that improves music Captioning through music–text alignment. For a given music, we generate a caption and reconstruct the music via a text-to-music model. We then measure the similarity between the original and reconstructed audio. Using this cycle consistency score, our approach: (1) constructs a large-scale preference dataset of over 410K pairs by ranking candidate outputs, (2) trains a reward model for evaluating captioning quality and modeling human preference, and (3) enables Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to improve captioning models without human annotation. Our approach improves music–text alignment, leading to more fine-grained music captions, and suggests that these improvements can further benefit both text-conditioned music generation and music captioning. We publicly release our dataset, model, and code at https://github.com/CapCyCin/CapCyCin/.

papers.title: Geometric Iterative Retrieval for Neural Audio Codec Resynthesis
papers.authors: Leo Schmidt-Traub; Frederic Berdoz; Luca A. Lanzendörfer; Roger Wattenhofer
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs based on Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) have become the dominant discrete representation for token-based general audio generation, yet resynthesizing high-quality audio from coarse codec tokens remains an open problem. Rather than classifying over discrete vocabularies or regressing to a single target vector, our method performs contrastive retrieval in the codebook's geometric space. We evaluate our approach on codec restoration tasks across speech and music, demonstrating improvements over both token prediction and one-step regression baselines.

papers.authors: Haven Kim; Yupeng Hou; Julian McAuley
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation systems have achieved significant advances by leveraging semantic IDs to represent items. To make the learned tokens stable across segmentation positions and small variations in timing and pitch range, we train the model with a reconstruction objective evaluated under the best alignment among a set of candidate temporal and pitch-domain transformations. Applied to Korean traditional music, the learned tokens recover information about expert-defined sigimsae categories without supervision, and in pansori individual tokens align with the two principal modes, Gyemyeonjo and Ujo, supporting their use as units for corpus-level analysis of contour-centric traditions.

Here, we propose VioTech, a frame-level violin technique detection framework that predicts techniques directly at 10 ms resolution without explicit note segmentation. To handle the large temporal-scale variation among techniques, VioTech combines a frozen MERT encoder with a multi-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture and task-specific routing for tonal, articulation, and legato-related predictions. We also introduce VioTech120, the first manually annotated dataset of violin playing techniques constructed from real solo performance recordings, as well as an accompanying note-labeling user interface. Results demonstrate that VioTech achieved consistent improvements over prior methods and significantly enhanced cross-dataset generalization, establishing a new state-of-the-art in violin technique-aware transcription.

papers.abstract: Automatic music transcription and score following have been extensively studied for piano, but violin remains underexplored. Weak onsets, continuous pitch variation from vibrato and portamento, limited training data, and frequent silences in ensemble settings make both tasks particularly challenging. Moreover, existing violin transcription models have mainly focused on offline processing, which limits their use in real-time applications. To address this gap, we propose STRAdi, a fully causal violin transcription model designed for streaming inference, and pair it with a symbolic tracker for real-time score following. Despite strict causality, STRAdi remains competitive with its offline non-causal counterpart. The resulting transcribe-and-track pipeline improves tracking robustness over audio-based baselines. In particular, the pipeline is more robust to violin-silent passages than audio-based trackers.

papers.abstract: Popular music circulates globally while being locally reinterpreted, yet this process of cross-cultural style diffusion has rarely been quantified. We propose an era-classification framework for measuring temporal alignment between chart cultures. CNN classifiers trained from scratch on Billboard Hot 100 audio are applied to Korean Melon chart songs. Korean chart songs from the 1960s through the 1980s are consistently inferred as belonging to earlier Billboard eras, by a median of about four to five years, while the same models remain unbiased on held-out Billboard audio. The offset then halves at the 1990s, to roughly two to three years, and holds there through the 2000s. Reverse inference shows a complementary narrowing, and the pattern holds across architectures and seeds. We interpret these results as reflecting how globally circulating pop styles were locally adopted and progressively synchronized. The framework can be applied to other pairs of chart cultures beyond the US–Korea case examined here.

To address the one-to-many mapping induced by the first challenge, we formulate synthesizer inversion as conditional generation over discrete synthesizer parameters and use masked discrete diffusion as the generator. This treatment additionally avoids the fixed-order assumption of autoregressive models and the continuous-relaxation mismatch of flow matching when modeling categorical synthesizer controls. To address the second challenge, we further fine-tune the model with GRPO-style audio-domain rewards computed from rendered outputs. Experiments on Dexed show that, after supervised training, the discrete diffusion model is competitive with autoregressive and flow-matching baselines, and reward-based fine-tuning further improves out-of-domain audio matching performance. Code and demos are available at: https://github.com/DDSynth-RL/DDSynthRL.

papers.title: Interpretable Inverse Acoustic Modeling of Percussion via Physics-Guided Spectral Decomposition
papers.authors: Rajeev Rajan; Kevin Benty; Athul Joe Joseph Palliparambil
papers.abstract: We propose a physics-based parametric framework for percussive instruments that acts as a digital twin, enabling sound synthesis through direct control of physical parameters such as membrane tension, strike position, and geometry. The model generates sound from first principles using eigenmodes of a non-uniform membrane, yielding a physically interpretable representation. We introduce Physics-Guided Spectral Decomposition (PGSD), an inverse method that aligns the model with observed audio via closed-form ridge regression, enabling estimation of modal amplitudes and underlying physical parameters. Experiments on synthetic data demonstrate physically consistent behavior under parameter variation, while evaluation on real Chenda recordings shows accurate reconstruction (coefficient of determination, R2 up to 0.8152) and consistent excitation trends. The proposed framework provides a unified, bidirectional approach for controllable synthesis and interpretable parameter inference without requiring training data.

papers.title: End-to-End Motif Discovery for Symbolic Polyphonic Music via Differentiable Label Propagation on Note-Pair Graphs
papers.authors: Raynaldi Lalang; Kazuyoshi Yoshii
papers.abstract: Symbolic polyphonic motif discovery is a nested partitioning problem that aims to find thematically important note sequences that repeat within a musical piece. A previous method attempts to learn motif characteristics at the note level and then performs pattern discovery as an independent point-set search with a fixed similarity rule. As such, the learned note filter and the fixed search are optimized separately, and the geometric search tends to produce more motif groups and occurrences than necessary. To solve this problem, we propose end-to-end differentiable training that uses a note-pair graph to learn affinities between neighboring notes and form motif occurrences. Annotated occurrences provide soft-membership seeds that propagate through the same affinities used at test time, and differentiable losses at the note-pair, occurrence, and motif-type levels train the affinities jointly. On the BPS-motif dataset (first movements of Beethoven's 32 piano sonatas), our method improved establishment F1 from 0.676 to 0.732 and three-layer F1 from 0.273 to 0.286, and cut occurrences per piece from 1181.1 to 105.1 (ground truth 154.5). Adding occurrence completion gave the highest occurrence precision and the lowest cluster impurity, and yielded 133.4 occurrences per piece.

Yet computational models of pianist body motion have so far addressed only hands or 2D upper bodies. We present Pianoid, the first 3D 26-joint pianist body motion system from MIDI. Pianoid is a four-stage hybrid pipeline whose body partition and diffusion placement are derived from a coupling analysis of the MOSA performance corpus. MPJPE (Mean Per Joint Position Error) rewards the near-static collapse of mean-regressed baselines. To surface this failure mode we report per-axis expressiveness ratios aggregated as Δ1, validated by a dual perceptual study (non-expert N=28, expert N=9). Non-expert viewers prefer Pianoid over every baseline and ablation, while still preferring the ground truth. Experts attribute the residual gap to fine timing and articulation rather than under-expression. papers.title: StemFX: Learning Mixing Style Representations via Autoregressive FX Chain Prediction on Source-Separated Stems
papers.authors: Yuan-Chiao Cheng; Jui-Te Wu; Brian Chen; Yen-Tung Yeh; Yu-Hua Chen; Yi-Hsuan Yang

papers.title: Mitigating Structural Collapse in Multi-Codebook Autoregressive Music Generation via Structure-Aware Scheduled Sampling
papers.authors: Chen Feng Tsai; Mi-Yen Yeh
papers.abstract: Hierarchical autoregressive music models suffer from "structural collapse" during long-horizon generation, caused by exposure bias compounding across the two-dimensional residual vector quantization (RVQ) grid. papers.title: Pitch Contour Tokenization using VQ-VAE and Its Application on Korean Traditional Music Analysis

papers.title: VioTech: Frame-Level Violin Playing Technique Detection with Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts
papers.authors: Ting-Kang Wang; Vincent K.M. Cheung; Nan-Tien Lai; Li Su

papers.title: STRAdi: Real-Time Violin Transcription for Score Following
papers.authors: Sein Lee; Jiyun Park; Juhan Nam
papers.abstract: Automatic music transcription and score following have been extensively studied for piano, but violin remains underexplored. papers.title: Measuring Cross-Cultural Style Diffusion Through Era Classification: US and Korean Popular Music
papers.authors: Dasol Lee; Minhee Lee; Seonguk Ju; Daewoong Kim; Harin Lee; Dasaem Jeong
papers.abstract: Popular music circulates globally while being locally reinterpreted, yet this process of cross-cultural style diffusion has rarely been quantified. papers.authors: Tristan WU); Daniel Chin; Junan Zhang; Junyan Jiang; Yansen Jing; Gus Xia

To address the one-to-many mapping induced by the first challenge, we formulate synthesizer inversion as conditional generation over discrete synthesizer parameters and use masked discrete diffusion as the generator. This treatment additionally avoids the fixed-order assumption of autoregressive models and the continuous-relaxation mismatch of flow matching when modeling categorical synthesizer controls. To address the second challenge, we further fine-tune the model with GRPO-style audio-domain rewards computed from rendered outputs. Experiments on Dexed show that, after supervised training, the discrete diffusion model is competitive with autoregressive and flow-matching baselines, and reward-based fine-tuning further improves out-of-domain audio matching performance. Code and demos are available at: https://github.com/DDSynth-RL/DDSynthRL.

papers.authors: Rajeev Rajan; Kevin Benty; Athul Joe Joseph Palliparambil

The proposed framework provides a unified, bidirectional approach for controllable synthesis and interpretable parameter inference without requiring training data.

papers.title: End-to-End Motif Discovery for Symbolic Polyphonic Music via Differentiable Label Propagation on Note-Pair Graphs
papers.authors: Raynaldi Lalang; Kazuyoshi Yoshii
papers.abstract: Symbolic polyphonic motif discovery is a nested partitioning problem that aims to find thematically important note sequences that repeat within a musical piece. papers.authors: Pablo Alonso-Jiménez; Xavier Lizarraga-Seijas; Xavier Serra; Dmitry Bogdanov
papers.abstract: Recent open text-audio contrastive models (CLAPs) are typically trained with LLM-generated captions derived from tag datasets or web search results, which tend to be accurate but expressively narrow. We find that album review supervision yields the largest retrieval gains on a human-written caption benchmark (Song Describer), particularly for complex queries that other existing caption datasets leave uncovered. In addition, we revisit the training recipe and show that SigReg regularization, which encourages an isotropic Gaussian distribution in the embedding space, improves MLP probing across classification tasks, as well as text-to-music retrieval. papers.title: Comparing Compression-Based Models of Similarity in Jazz Harmonic Progressions
papers.authors: Xinyi Guan; Edward T. R. Hall; Zeng Ren; Marina Borsodi-Benson; Claire Pelofi; Martin Rohrmeier
papers.abstract: The ability to accurately account for musical similarity is essential to a wide range of tasks in MIR and cognition. Compression distance provides a promising and underexplored model for similarity: two pieces are similar to the extent that a compact description of one helps describe the other. This paper investigates two competing compression strategies, focusing on surface and structural regularities, respectively. The first estimates how predictable one sequence is under a probabilistic model trained on another using the Prediction by Partial Matching algorithm. The second approach measures how much a piece's derivation tree can be simplified with the learned abstractions from another, using a library-learning algorithm (Stitch). Given a collection of derivation trees, it treats each instance as a program and compresses the collection by learning a library of reusable program abstractions that capture recurring substructures and rewriting the programs in terms of these abstractions. We apply both models to a corpus of jazz harmony analyses and measure their compression performance, comparing interaction between the two. We further present qualitative analyses to demonstrate where the models diverge and agree.

papers.authors: Hewei Gao; Tim Beyer; Xiaoxuan Wang; Martin Rohrmeier
papers.abstract: Roman Numeral Analysis (RNA) is often cast as a classification task, yet it is inherently interpretive: multiple analyses may be musically plausible, and their value often depends not only on the labels themselves but also on the reasoning and analytical perspective that support them. In this work, we present RNGen, a large language model approach to Roman Numeral Analysis in symbolic music, as a first step toward such systems. RNGen bridges a symbolic music encoder and a large language model through a lightweight projector, adapting a vision-language-style architecture to harmonic analysis. To make this bridge effective, we introduce a series of music-specific adaptations spanning representation design, musically informed data processing, and staged multi-task fine-tuning. Experiments show that this encoder-to-LLM approach can model RNA competitively, and ablations confirm the importance of these adaptations. We position RNGen not as a completed solution to explainable RNA, since it does not yet produce validated explanations, but as the first LLM-based foundation for it: a framework that demonstrates the feasibility of LLM-based Roman Numeral Analysis from symbolic music and provides a foundation for future systems that can support analytical conclusions with musically meaningful justifications. papers.authors: Marco Pasini; Javier Nistal; Cyran Aouameur; Stefan Lattner; György Fazekas
papers.abstract: We introduce AudioCodex, a fully causal autoencoder for live generative audio applications that compresses stereo audio into compact continuous latent sequences at ∼10 Hz. It combines a Mean Flow magnitude autoencoder with latent hypersphere projection, bounded-noise augmentation, representation alignment, and adversarial phase recovery to learn representations that support both efficient downstream generation and high-quality reconstruction. Through extensive ablations, we show that AudioCodex outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of generation-reconstruction trade-off, whilst remaining strictly causal in both encoding and decoding. This work paves the way towards truly real-time interactive and streaming generative audio applications. Supplementary results and audio samples are available in the website.

papers.authors: Emile Dugelay; Thomas Barand; Aurélien Laouar; Baptiste Campeas; Darius Afchar; Romain Hennequin
papers.abstract: AI music generators leave predictable spectral artifacts determined by their architecture. Existing detectors exploit these artifacts with near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks, but their performance collapses under simple audio manipulations, such as speed modification or pitch shifting. We address this open robustness problem by introducing a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline that aims to prevent this kind of attack by design. Our method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via a log-STFT remapping. A single learned cross-correlation filter, combined with max-pooling, provides shift invariance at inference time. Training uses a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization, regularizing boundary weights. Because robustness to speed change is built in by design, the detector is also interpretable: it outputs both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing have improved lyrics-based music genre classification through large language models, yet such black box systems obscure the actual linguistic style differences between music genres. Interpretable approaches in computational musicology and MIR, meanwhile, often relied on either formal structural analysis of lyrics or on topic or sentiment analyses. However, the significant recovery of text-derived labels indicates that affective distinctions encoded in Metastasio's aria texts remain detectable across diverse musical settings despite compositional variance.

These findings suggest that single-label evaluation may underestimate valid human judgements and motivate richer annotation and evaluation schemes for the task.

papers.abstract: AI music generators leave predictable spectral artifacts determined by their architecture. Existing detectors exploit these artifacts with near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks, but their performance collapses under simple audio manipulations, such as speed modification or pitch shifting. We address this open robustness problem by introducing a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline that aims to prevent this kind of attack by design. Our method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via a log-STFT remapping. A single learned cross-correlation filter, combined with max-pooling, provides shift invariance at inference time. Training uses a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization, regularizing boundary weights. Because robustness to speed change is built in by design, the detector is also interpretable: it outputs both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

papers.authors: Markus Radke; Steffen Lepa
papers.abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing have improved lyrics-based music genre classification through large language models, yet such black box systems obscure the actual linguistic style differences between music genres. However, genre-typical formulaic expressions, though deemed relevant in popular music studies, have hardly been investigated at all. Our study contributes to filling this gap by uncovering genre discriminative lyrical style patterns—topics, sentiments, and formulaic expressions—in fifty years of Anglophone German popular music. Using the POPTRAG corpus and Discogs genre annotations for 126,042 tracks with English lyrics, we apply the fightin' words method to identify statistically distinctive n-grams across genres. We then identify latent topics, sentiments, and types of formulaic expressions from these via structural topic modeling using training corpus target genres as prevalence covariates. Resulting interpretable lyrics features are employed in machine-learning models that reveal the function of stylistic markers for specific popular music genres. Our transparent ML method approaches the predictive performance of a transfer-learned DistilBERT classifier while offering conceptual insight into how lyrics encode genre identity.

Classification skill is assessed using symbolic music features under aria-grouped cross-validation, normalised against a stratified dummy baseline. While human schemes yield statistically significant but modest predictive signal (skill=0.024-0.045), Gemma 3 re-annotation more than doubles this performance. Notably, the best-performing conditions across historically motivated and LLM-proposed taxonomies achieve skill comparable to human schemes, suggesting that composers' choices reflect textual affect under multiple taxonomy designs with capable annotation. Negative silhouette coefficients across all conditions indicate that affective categories do not form geometrically coherent clusters, suggesting that Baroque composers realised the same affect through musically heterogeneous strategies. In this paper, we present, to our knowledge, the first systematic study of human performance on lyric-based topic classification and compare it with a logistic regression baseline on the same dataset. We conduct an online annotation study in which participants assign three ranked topic labels to songs based solely on their lyrics. We evaluate inter-annotator agreement, as well as individual and aggregated human accuracy against Songfacts-derived ground truth labels. The results show that lyric topic classification is challenging and inherently subjective. Specifically, individual annotators match the gold label 28% of the time (53% within their top three), comparable to an automatic baseline (27%/48%); aggregated human judgements reach 42%/69%, exceeding the strongest automatic configuration on the same songs in top-3 accuracy (33%/63%). Inter-annotator agreement is low to moderate (pairwise τ = 0.29–0.38) but rises consistently when measured against group consensus (τ = 0.40–0.51), indicating that annotators diverge in the details within a partially shared interpretation. These findings suggest that single-label evaluation may underestimate valid human judgements and motivate richer annotation and evaluation schemes for the task.

papers.title: Learning to Predict Performance-induced Emotion Differences in Classical Piano Music
papers.authors: Joann Ching; Gerhard Widmer
papers.abstract: Music is often used as a medium for communicating emotion, with performers shaping perceived affect through interpretation. This study addresses the challenge of identifying and predicting subtle changes in perceived emotion that are exclusively due to differences in performance. We focus on classical solo piano music, using a set of 6 commercial recordings of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier Book I, annotated in terms of valence and arousal. By encoding the recordings through performance-specific features only, we isolate performance information from aspects of the composition itself, which tend to dominate the overall perceived emotional category. A preliminary analysis validates that these features vary meaningfully across performers. We then propose a relative regression framework, Delta-VA, to predict deviations in valence-arousal relative to an “average” performance, thereby focusing on the changes in emotion brought about by a specific way of playing a piece. In addition to the standard R2 regression score, we introduce geometric evaluation metrics to assess the preservation of pairwise differences between performances. Results indicate high directional consistency with the ground truth, but also a compression in prediction magnitude, indicating that the model tends to underestimate expressive performance effects.

papers.title: Diff2Mix: Controllable Music Mixing via Diffusion Models and Differentiable Audio Effects
papers.authors: Yisu Zong; Jinjie Shi; Joshua Reiss
papers.abstract: Automatic music mixing aims to combine multitrack audio into a balanced and coherent musical piece. Because the content of different songs and the subjective preferences of mixing engineers jointly shape the final outcome, a practical system should deliver well-balanced mixes while allowing for controllable stylistic variation. However, most existing methods treat automatic mixing and mixing style control as separate tasks, making it difficult for a single system to produce high-quality mixes while remaining editable and style-aware. To address this limitation, this paper presents Diff2Mix, a generative automatic mixing system based on diffusion models and a differentiable mixing console. This system offers two levels of optional user control: a reference song enables overall production style control, and the differentiable mixing console provides explicit audio effects parameters for interpretability and fine-grained optimization. We demonstrate our system’s competitive performance through both objective and subjective evaluations in terms of mixing quality and control ability.

papers.authors: Jiarui Li; Mark Liberman
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as zero-shot tools for symbolic music style transfer. The attractor's location depends on the cycle's starting style, and in cross-cultural cycles this produces a clear asymmetry: the final endpoint shifts are consistent with model-family-specific style priors. papers.title: Inferring Implied Harmonies through Voice Leading in Monophonic Instrumental Music Using Graph-Based Methods
papers.authors: Marina Borsodi-Benson; Martin Rohrmeier

papers.authors: Tobias Hornbogen; Josef Valentin

papers.authors: Angelos-Nikolaos Kanatas; Yuexuan Kong; Pablo Alonso-Jiménez; Xavier Serra; Dmitry Bogdanov
papers.abstract: Music foundation models are commonly used as frozen audio feature extractors, yet selecting which layer to extract from remains largely heuristic. papers.title: A Cross-Cultural Dataset of Instrumental Difficulty for Woodwinds and Strings
papers.authors: Rui Yang; Mathieu Giraud; Florence Levé
papers.abstract: The difficulty of a musical score depends partly on the instrument on which a musician plays it. papers.authors: François Rigaud; Gabriel Meseguer Brocal; Benjamin Martin; Romain Hennequin

papers.authors: Arhan Vohra; Choenden Kyirong; Laura Ibañez; Martín Rocamora

papers.authors: Yan-Martin Tamm; Anna Aljanaki
papers.abstract: Listener preferences are influenced by multiple factors including sound (timbre, rhythm, harmony), text (lyrics and their emotional and social implications), and social context (popularity, genre identity, the image of the artist). If DTW has found a very prominent path, then if we re-run the alignment with relaxed boundary conditions, it will still pick the same path. If, on the other hand, DTW has found a “weak” path, then re-running the alignment with relaxed boundary conditions will likely yield a different path. Accordingly, our reliability metric is computed by picking a local section of the DTW alignment path, re-estimating the alignment with FlexDTW (which allows flexibility in the boundary conditions), and then measuring how well the DTW and FlexDTW paths agree. We assess the proposed reliability metric on DTW alignment paths containing both matching and non-matching regions across a range of scenarios on an audio-audio alignment task. We find that the reliability metric correctly identifies reliable regions of the alignment path with an aggregate AUROC of 0.97. This approach provides an unsupervised method for estimating the reliability of a DTW alignment path.

At inference time, LOUDAR alternates between estimating the clean latent variable and updating the latent operator parameters. An unconditional latent diffusion model provides a prior over clean audio and regularizes this inference by steering the latent estimate toward the manifold of clean recordings. Because the degradation model is adapted per input, the approach is broadly applicable across diverse restoration problems. We evaluate LOUDAR on singing voice effect removal and restoration, as well as guitar distortion removal, and show that it consistently improves over degraded inputs and is competitive with supervised and unsupervised baselines in waveform and latent domains.

Being model-agnostic, the framework is compatible with any pre-trained diffusion model operating in either the waveform or latent domain. Objective evaluations demonstrate that SimDPS outperforms widely adopted RePaint and DPS methods across acoustic features and neural-embedding distance metrics. Subjective evaluations on multi-genre music datasets confirm that SimDPS enhances perceptual plausibility compared to previous diffusion-based methods and demonstrates robustness to poorly matched similarity candidates. These findings pave the way for improved music restoration and context-aware audio editing.

Both models achieve near-perfect performance on CFM but degrade substantially under synthetic broadcast conditions. Broadcast-oriented training improves robustness compared with clean training, although performance remains limited. On RTB, evaluated using BAMM, both models degrade further and show substantial score overlap between AI-generated and human-made music. These results expose a critical domain gap and show that current training approaches on CNN-based detectors remain insufficient for reliable AI-generated music detection in broadcast monitoring.

We introduce InvFlowFD, which performs flow inversion and compares a group of inverted samples to the prior distribution. We evaluate our method against prior work, quantitatively and with a thorough human study. Results suggest that InvFlowFD is highly correlated with human perception of sound distortions, as well as generative models' quality, while being more flexible and less restrictive than existing metrics.
